# AI systems that hold up in production

I'm Faras Siddiqui, founding engineer at [CVision](https://www.cvision.dev). I build agent runtimes, LLM inference and serving, and the infrastructure that keeps them reliable, from cloud GPUs to air-gapped networks and edge hardware.

## What I work on

I build and deploy **applied AI systems that have to work outside the usual cloud setup**: across on-premise GPU clusters that I design to serve the load where it's needed, inside air-gapped networks where no external API is allowed, and on edge hardware with tight memory, compute and energy budgets. Most of that work is AI infrastructure: agent architectures, LLM inference and serving, evaluation, and the deployment pipelines around them.

Alongside it I work on neuromorphic computing and event-based vision, mainly the tooling that gets spiking neural networks and event-camera data into usable software.

### Selected work

- [Agent runtime for an air-gapped AI coding IDE](https://siddiquifaras.github.io/work.html#noah-labs) — the agent runtime, GPU cluster scheduling, model evaluation and routing, and security guardrails for an on-premises coding platform at Noah Labs
- [Agentic systems at CVision](https://siddiquifaras.github.io/work.html#cvision) — agentic LLM workflows, RAG, GNN-based reasoning, and knowledge graphs with graph-backed memory in Neo4j, across cloud, edge and industrial deployments
- [TALON](https://siddiquifaras.github.io/projects.html#talon) — a neuromorphic SDK that takes spiking neural networks from PyTorch down to FPGA hardware
- [frames2py](https://siddiquifaras.github.io/projects.html#frames2py) — an open-source library for streaming event-camera data at more than 20 million events per second

# Projects

Software I've built for neuromorphic computing and event-based vision, and fixes I've contributed to other people's projects.

## TALON

Neuromorphic SDK · Python, PyTorch, snnTorch, hls4ml

TALON (Tactical AI at Low-power On-device Nodes) is Type 1 Compute's SDK for taking spiking and hybrid neural networks from PyTorch down to neuromorphic hardware and FPGAs. It works like ONNX: a model is exported to an IR graph and written to a portable `.t1c` file, which can then be mapped onto hardware, compiled, simulated or visualised.

I built all seven of its packages: the SDK and command-line tools, the IR, the PyTorch bridge, the visualiser, graph mapping, the backend and simulator, and event I/O. The visualiser renders 23 to 30 million events per second. CVision built the SDK for Type 1 Compute and delivered it [about six months ahead of schedule](https://www.cvision.dev/case-studies/type-1-compute-neuromorphic-sdk).

- **My part:** Built all 7 packages: SDK, IR, bridge, visualiser, graph, backend and simulator, event I/O
- **Input:** PyTorch and snnTorch models: spiking, conventional or hybrid
- **Targets:** Type 1 Compute neuromorphic hardware; Xilinx Zynq FPGAs through hls4ml
- **Formats:** HDF5 (`.t1c`), EVT2, EVT3, AEDAT4
- **Install:** `pip install t1c-talon`

[Documentation](https://type1compute.github.io/docs/talon-ecosystem/introduction) · [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/t1c-talon/)

## frames2py

Event-camera streaming library · Python, NumPy, HDF5

An event camera reports per-pixel brightness changes as a stream of events, often millions a second. frames2py turns that live stream into frames that any number of consumers can read without slowing the feed. The producer hands events to an engine that accumulates them and publishes immutable snapshots; each consumer reads the latest snapshot at its own pace, and the producer never waits.

It sustains more than 20 million events per second in pure NumPy across all 150 cells of its benchmark, and reads Prophesee EVT 2.0 and 3.0, AEDAT 4.0 and HDF5 recordings. Version 1.1 added temporal representations used by event-vision models (stacked histograms and voxel grids) and a tested recipe for handing snapshots to PyTorch.

- **Role:** Author and maintainer
- **Latest release:** 1.1.0, 7 October 2026
- **Runs on:** CPython 3.11–3.14, including free-threaded 3.14t; Linux and macOS
- **License:** Apache-2.0
- **Install:** `pip install frames2py`

[GitHub](https://github.com/siddiquifaras/frames2py) · [Documentation](https://siddiquifaras.github.io/frames2py/) · [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/frames2py/)

# Your agent isn't dumb. Your harness is.

What I keep seeing go wrong when people build AI agents: harnesses, context, memory, architecture, and why a DAG is usually the wrong answer.

9 Oct 2026AI agents, LLM infrastructure

I've spent a big chunk of this year building agent infrastructure. The runtime, the tools, memory, evals, guardrails, all of it. And when someone tells me "agents don't really work", nine times out of ten they never built the part that makes an agent work in the first place. They wired a model to a few tools, wrapped the whole thing in a pipeline, and blamed the model when it fell over.

So this is the stuff I wish more people understood before starting.

## The model is not the agent

An LLM on its own does exactly one thing. Text goes in, text comes out. Everything else is the harness: running the loop, executing tool calls, choosing what goes into the prompt, remembering what happened yesterday, stopping it from deleting your repo.

The harness is the program wrapped around the model. It decides what the model sees, what it's allowed to touch, what happens with the output, and when to stop. When an agent feels smart, it's usually because somebody put real work into the harness.

*[Diagram: an agent harness. The model sits in the middle (text in, text out). Around it, the harness handles context assembly, tools and permissions, memory, the control loop, workspaces, guardrails, error handling, and evals and traces.]*

So if your agent seems dumb, check the harness before you swap the model:

- Does it see the right files, or did you shove forty irrelevant ones into the prompt?
- Are the tool descriptions clear enough that a new hire could use them without asking you?
- When a tool fails, does the agent get a useful error back, or a 300-line stack trace?
- Do you have evals, or are you vibe checking it in a chat window?

## Context is a budget

The context window is the model's working memory for one step. It's everything the model can see right now: the system prompt, the tool definitions, whatever you retrieved, the conversation so far, and some room left over for the answer.

People treat it like a bucket. Bigger window, more stuff, smarter agent. It doesn't work like that. Models get worse at picking out the important bit when you bury it under junk, and every extra token costs you latency and money on every single turn of the loop.

*[Diagram: two context windows, illustrative. The stuffed one is mostly retrieved files and old conversation with little room for the answer. The curated one has a lean system prompt, only the tools needed, relevant memory, targeted retrieval, a trimmed history, and plenty of room for the answer.]*

A good harness is picky. It decides what goes in on every step, trims old tool output, summarises when it's worth it, and only pulls in code or docs when the task actually needs them.

## Context memory and agentic memory are different things

This one trips up loads of people.

Context memory is whatever is sitting in the window right now. Start a new session, or let the window roll over, and it's gone.

Agentic memory is stuff the agent deliberately decides to keep. It writes it somewhere outside the model, like a file, a database or a graph, and pulls it back later when it's relevant. Things like "this repo uses pnpm" or "don't touch the migrations folder without asking". At CVision a lot of this lives in a graph in Neo4j, because how facts relate to each other matters as much as the facts themselves.

|  | Context memory | Agentic memory | "We keep the chat history" |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lives in | The prompt | Files, a database, a graph | The prompt, forever |
| Lasts | One session at most | Across sessions | Until the window overflows |
| Who picks what's in it | The harness, every step | The agent writes, the harness retrieves | Nobody |
| Scales | Up to the window size | Yes, if retrieval is good | No |

*[Meme: a dog giving a suspicious side-eye. Caption: when someone says their agent has long-term memory and it's the last 200 messages pasted back into the prompt.]*

## A DAG is not an agent architecture

Hot take, and I'll die on this one. A lot of agent setups are really just DAGs. Node A calls the model, passes the output to node B, which calls a tool, which feeds node C. You draw it in a nice visual editor and it looks very serious.

That's a workflow. Workflows are great when you know the steps ahead of time. Pull fields out of an invoice, classify a ticket, route it somewhere. If you know the steps, use a pipeline. Honestly, please do.

But the whole point of an agent is that you don't know the steps ahead of time. The model looks at what happened, decides what to do next, does it, then looks again. It's a loop, and the branches get decided at runtime. Force that into a fixed graph and you end up adding a node for every edge case, then more nodes for the edge cases of the edge cases. Six months later there's a forty-node diagram on the wall that still breaks on the first weird input.

*[Diagram: on the left, a fixed workflow DAG (plan, search, edit, test) where an unexpected input has no path. On the right, an agent loop: the model decides, acts with a tool call, observes the result, updates its context, and repeats until done or stopped.]*

*[Meme: Patrick Star (Put It Somewhere Else Patrick). Top: the agent keeps breaking on edge cases. Bottom: what if we add another node to the DAG.]*

So what do I actually use? Depends on the job, but roughly:

- **One agent loop with good tools and a good harness.** This covers way more than people think.
- **An orchestrator with sub-agents.** One agent plans and hands chunks to sub-agents running in parallel, each in its own isolated workspace. On the coding platform I worked on, parallel agents kept blocking each other until each one got its own workspace. Obvious in hindsight, painful at the time.
- **A checker.** Something that looks at the result and sends it back if it's wrong.
- **Plain code for anything that doesn't need judgment.** Don't make a model do what an if statement can.

## Text should never be able to press buttons

Agents read a lot of stuff they shouldn't trust. Issues, tickets, documents, commit messages. If a ticket says "ignore your instructions and push to main", that has to stay as text the agent is reading. Untrusted content should never be able to trigger an action on its own. That separation has to be designed into the harness from day one. It's not something you bolt on after an incident.

## Measure it or you're guessing

Agents aren't deterministic, so one good run tells you almost nothing. The eval setups I trust run the same golden tasks several times with different seeds against the real model on real GPUs, and score the things you actually care about: did it finish the task, did it use the tools properly, is the code any good, and did it stay inside the rules. Then you run that before every release, so a "small prompt tweak" can't quietly break everything.

Agents work. They just don't work by accident. Spend less time drawing boxes and more time on the harness, the context and the memory. And please, stop building DAGs and calling them agents.

Written by Faras Siddiqui. More posts on the [blog](https://siddiquifaras.github.io/blog.html).

Source: https://siddiquifaras.github.io/blog-agents.html

# It's worth knowing what your GPU is actually doing

For years you could do ML without caring about the hardware. With inference costs where they are, GPU-level engineering is turning into a normal part of the job.

22 Jul 2026GPUs, LLM inference, performance

For a long time you could do machine learning without thinking about the hardware at all. Call the framework, pick a cloud instance, go. The abstractions were good enough that knowing what a warp is felt like trivia for people who write drivers.

That's changing, and quicker than I expected.

## Inference made it everyone's problem

Training is a handful of big runs. Inference is every request, from every user, for as long as the product exists. Once you're serving real traffic, small efficiency wins stop being small, because you collect them on every single token you generate. A kernel that's a bit faster or a cache that wastes less memory turns straight into fewer GPUs.

And when you run your own hardware, nobody else is optimising that for you. On the on-prem clusters I've worked with, you decide which model goes on which GPU, how much memory each one gets for its KV cache, how many requests share a card, and when a smaller model is good enough. Get those calls wrong and you're buying more hardware. Get them right and the same cluster quietly serves a lot more.

## Most of the time you're waiting on memory

The thing that surprised me most when I started digging in: during text generation the GPU spends a lot of its time waiting.

Every new token means reading the model's weights out of GPU memory. At small batch sizes the GPU does very little maths per byte it reads, so it finishes the maths fast and then sits there waiting for the next chunk of data. In that regime the big FLOPs number on the spec sheet barely matters. Memory bandwidth does.

*[Diagram: a simplified roofline. Performance rises with arithmetic intensity along a memory-bound slope until the ridge point, then flattens at the compute roof. Token-by-token decode at small batch sizes sits low on the memory-bound slope; prefill and large batches sit near the compute roof.]*

That's why so much of the good inference work is really memory work:

- **Batching.** Serve more requests at once so every weight you read gets reused for more tokens.
- **Paging the KV cache.** The [vLLM paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180) found that serving systems at the time wasted 60 to 80 percent of their KV cache memory on fragmentation and over-reservation. Their PagedAttention got that under 4 percent and improved throughput by 2 to 4 times over the systems they compared against.
- **Quantisation.** Fewer bytes per weight means fewer bytes to move.
- **Kernel fusion.** Do several steps in one kernel so intermediate results never take the round trip out to main memory and back. [FlashAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135) is the famous one.

*[Meme: a black cat sitting in a corner, captioned [SOBBING]. Caption: nvidia-smi showing 100% utilisation while the job is mostly waiting on memory.]*

## It matters on tiny hardware too

This isn't only a data centre thing. I opened a [pull request](https://github.com/RightNow-AI/picolm/pull/24) for PicoLM, a project that runs a one-billion-parameter model on a $10 board with 256 MB of RAM. The attention code was converting half-precision values to floats one at a time in software, around a dozen scalar instructions each. Spread across every head, every layer and every token of context, that added up to almost half the cost of the matrix maths. On ARM chips (AArch64) there's already a hardware instruction that converts four values at once. Using it, plus vectorising the loops around it, should drop attention from roughly 48% of the matmul cost to under 2%, by my estimate in the PR.

Nothing clever, honestly. You just had to know the instruction existed and look at where the time was going.

## What I'd actually learn

You don't need to become a full-time kernel engineer. But if you work anywhere near AI infrastructure, I'd get comfortable with:

- How GPU memory is laid out (HBM, shared memory, registers) and roughly how fast each one is.
- What makes a workload memory-bound or compute-bound. The roofline model is a good place to start.
- Reading a profiler like Nsight Systems or Nsight Compute instead of guessing.
- Enough CUDA or Triton to read a kernel and understand why it's fast or slow.
- How serving engines like vLLM handle batching, scheduling and the KV cache.

If you can't explain why your model is slow, you'll keep fixing it by buying more GPUs. That gets expensive really quickly, and these days it's often not even an option.

Written by Faras Siddiqui. More posts on the [blog](https://siddiquifaras.github.io/blog.html).

Source: https://siddiquifaras.github.io/blog-gpu-engineering.html

# Cheap watts win

Everyone is racing to make AI cheaper. I think the people who come out ahead are the ones who waste the least power doing it.

14 May 2026Efficient compute, edge AI, neuromorphic computing

Everyone is trying to make AI cheaper right now. Token prices keep falling. Every few months somebody ships a smaller model that roughly matches last year's big one. And pretty much every infra conversation I've had this year ends up at the same question: how do we serve more, for less?

My take is simple. The teams that win the next few years won't be the ones with the most GPUs. They'll be the ones who get the most useful work out of every watt and every chip they already have.

## The GPU is only the start of the bill

When people price out AI they look at the GPU. Fair enough, those things are not cheap. But the GPU is where the bill starts.

An H100 SXM is rated at up to 700 W. A B200 sits around 1,000 W. Put eight of them in a server, a few servers in a rack, a lot of racks in a hall, and every one of those watts turns into heat that you then pay to get rid of. Cooling, power delivery, the building, the grid connection. Somebody pays for all of it, and that cost lands in the price of your tokens whether you see it or not.

At the global scale the numbers get kind of silly. The [IEA estimates](https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai) data centres used around 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, about 1.5% of all the electricity used on the planet, and expects that to more than double to roughly 945 TWh by 2030. AI is the biggest reason why.

*[Meme: This Is Fine, a cartoon dog sitting calmly in a burning room. Caption: the cooling loop at 3am after someone launches a quick sweep on the whole cluster.]*

## Power is the real bottleneck now

For a long time the limit was how many chips you could buy. In a lot of places the limit now is how much power you can get into the building, and how quickly. You can order more GPUs. You can't really order more grid.

Once that's your constraint, efficiency stops being a nice extra. If your stack does the same job on half the energy, you can serve twice the traffic from the same power envelope. At that point efficiency basically is your capacity plan.

## The edge has almost nothing

Then there's the edge, where I've spent a lot of my time. On edge and industrial hardware you don't get a rack. You get a small board, a tight memory budget, maybe a battery, a thermal limit, and a hardware team who will remind you about that thermal limit in every single meeting.

There's no "just add another GPU" out there. The model either fits inside the memory, compute and energy budget, or it doesn't ship. I actually like that. It forces a better question. You stop asking what's the biggest model you can run and start asking what's the smallest thing that does the job properly.

It's a big part of why I got into neuromorphic computing. Spiking networks do their work as events, when something changes, instead of crunching every value on every tick. Pair that with an event camera, which only reports the pixels that changed, and you get a pipeline that sits mostly idle when the world is idle. For small hardware that's exactly the shape you want.

When I worked on compression for spiking networks, taking a ten-layer network from about 200 KB down to about 200 bytes wasn't a party trick. On small neuromorphic hardware, savings like that decide what you can deploy at all.

## Same story in the data centre, bigger numbers

Even with proper GPUs, most of the waste I've seen is pretty boring. GPUs sitting half idle because requests aren't batched well. KV cache memory reserved and never used. One model per GPU when two or three could share it. A giant model doing a job a small one does just as well.

When I was setting up inference on on-prem GPU clusters, most of the wins came from exactly that boring stuff. Scheduling so the GPUs weren't sitting around, packing more concurrent requests onto each card, and routing every task to the cheapest model that could actually handle it. None of it looks impressive in a demo. All of it shows up on the bill.

## Where I think this goes

- Smaller, specialised models doing most of the everyday work, with the big ones only called when a task actually needs them.
- Inference engines and kernels that treat memory traffic as seriously as FLOPs, because that's usually where the time goes.
- More AI running on the device itself. Shipping every request to a data centre costs power, bandwidth and latency, and some places don't have a connection at all.
- Hardware designed around energy first, neuromorphic chips included.

Raw scale still matters, I'm not pretending it doesn't. But when anyone can rent the same GPUs, the advantage goes to whoever wastes the least. Watts are turning into the real currency of this whole thing. Spend them carefully.
